title: ETX5900 S2 2026 quiz bank: adaptation for the ETX1100 eight-week intensive
text:
The source bank has 11 original weeks, usually 20 questions each. S3 Q7 below means Question 7 in source Week 3, not intensive Week 3. It contains marked answers and should remain an instructor source file. Keep means the statistical task is suitable; all retained questions still need answers and solution cues removed before student release. Adapt means retain the skill but replace data, context, or wording. Exclude means omit from the core eight-week quizzes.
The original Elecmart, Hytex, PlanFinan, Health care, Hospital Quality, and Data for quiz 11 workbooks were not found in this project. The embedded tables and image references in the Markdown file do supply some questions without those workbooks. title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Today’s journey

Select methods from a business question and variable types.
Analyse ETF’s supermarket staffing and profit case.
Turn output into recommendations and limitations.
Correct common statistical misconceptions.
Consolidate the six learning outcomes for the examination.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
The four purposes








Purpose
Core question
Example method




Describe
What happened in this sample?
tables, charts, summaries


Infer
What does the sample suggest about a population?
intervals, tests


Predict
What outcome is expected for given inputs?
regression


Decide
Which listed feasible option performs best?
ToolPak regression plus an Excel formula model

section: Watch me: unpack a business question

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Now you try: method selection





Choose a purpose and method for each question:

What percentage of stores open 24 hours?
Is population mean service quality above 80?
Which staffing factors predict profit?
Which listed price gives the highest predicted profit within a capacity limit?

Justify each choice from the variables and claim.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Business context
A supermarket chain is considering incentives intended to improve store performance.
Open week8-case-data.xlsx.
Each row represents a store. Variables cover:

profit and operating context;
manager and crew tenure;
manager and crew skill; and
service quality.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Staffing questions
The ETF case asks:

Are manager and crew skills associated?
Do crews stay longer where managers stay longer?
Are skill measures associated with service quality?
Is service quality associated with profit?

These are observational association questions—not experiments.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Watch me: correlation matrix
Use Data → Data Analysis → Correlation for selected numerical variables.

Include labels.
Confirm the output is symmetric with 1s on the diagonal.
Pair strong correlations with scatterplots.
Describe direction, strength, form, and unusual points.
Avoid ranking variables by correlation alone.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
High service-quality stores
ETF defines excellent service as ServQual >= 90.
Comparing skill across this threshold can be useful descriptively, but dichotomising a numerical variable discards information. Use it to complement—not replace—the continuous analysis.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
section: Now you try: compare service groups
text:
Now you try: compare service groups





Create an ExcellentService flag and compare CrewSkill and MgrSkill across groups.
Use appropriate centre, spread, and plots. State what the comparison suggests and why it does not establish that skill caused service quality.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Model service quality
Begin with a focused explanatory question:
ServQual_i=\beta_0+\beta_1MTenure_i+\beta_2CTenure_i+\beta_3MgrSkill_i+\beta_4CrewSkill_i+\varepsilon_i.
The chosen variables should reflect a rationale, not merely every available column.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Watch me: service-quality model

Fit the model in Excel.
Write the fitted equation.
Interpret two partial slopes.
Evaluate adjusted R^2 and Significance F.
Inspect coefficient p-values and residual plots.
Record limitations before considering reduction.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
section: Now you try: refine the service model
text:
Now you try: refine the service model





Create one defensible reduced model.
Compare it with the full model using coefficient stability, adjusted R^2, standard error, individual tests, overall evidence, residuals, and interpretability. Recommend one model.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Model profit in context
Profit may depend on staffing and store environment. Candidate predictors include tenure, skills, service quality, population, competition, visibility, pedestrian count, residential context, and 24-hour operation.
Adding controls can change staffing coefficients because store context is not evenly distributed.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Watch me: profit model
Build a full model with a clearly stated rationale.

Identify dummy-variable coding.
Interpret staffing slopes conditionally.
Distinguish statistical from practical significance.
Check overall fit and residuals.
Consider whether correlated predictors make individual coefficients unstable.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Evidence chain
A defensible recommendation connects:
question → data → method → result → limitation → action
Weak reports jump directly from a significant coefficient to a policy. Strong reports explain the comparison, uncertainty, assumptions, feasible action, and what should be tested next.

text:
Watch me: carry a ToolPak model into a decision
Suppose a pricing pilot covering AUD 50–105 gives the fitted equation
\widehat{Units}=701-5.01\times Price.
Before recommending a price, identify which numbers came from the Analysis ToolPak and which business inputs are still needed. State the observed price range and the production rule you would check.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
section: Now you try: compare feasible prices
text:
Now you try: compare feasible prices





Compare listed prices AUD 80, 90, and 100. Assume unit cost AUD 40, fixed cost AUD 1,200, and capacity 340 units.
For each price calculate predicted units, whole units planned after the capacity rule, revenue, cost, and profit. Recommend one listed price and explain one way the recommendation could change if the assumptions are wrong.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Misconception 1: conditional probability
“Because 70% of app users are highly satisfied, 70% of highly satisfied customers use the app.”
The statement reverses the condition:
P(Satisfied\mid App)\ne P(App\mid Satisfied).
The denominators differ.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
section: Now you try: correct the conditional claim
text:
Now you try: correct the conditional claim





Rewrite the claim correctly and describe the additional contingency-table information needed to calculate the reversed conditional probability.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Misconception 2: confidence intervals
“There is a 95% probability that this fixed population mean is inside our calculated interval.”
Frequentist confidence attaches 95% to the long-run method, not a probability assigned to the fixed parameter after observing the interval.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
section: Now you try: repair the interval statement
text:
Now you try: repair the interval statement





Write a correct contextual interpretation and explain why the interval does not describe where 95% of individual customers lie.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Misconception 3: regression coefficients
“The manager-skill coefficient is the raw difference in profit between high- and low-skill stores.”
In multiple regression it is a conditional comparison, holding other included predictors constant. Its unit and coding must be stated.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
section: Now you try: repair the coefficient claim
text:
Now you try: repair the coefficient claim





Choose one coefficient from your profit model and provide:

a correct interpretation;
the base category if relevant; and
one reason it should not be described as causal.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Misconception 4: evidence and importance
“Because p<0.05, the effect is large, useful, and the null hypothesis has a less than 5% chance of being true.”
A p-value addresses compatibility with H_0 under assumptions. Effect size, uncertainty, costs, and practical thresholds require separate evidence.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
section: Now you try: repair the evidence claim

Scatterplots first
A scatterplot reveals:

direction: positive or negative;
form: linear or nonlinear;
strength: tight or diffuse pattern; and
unusual observations: outliers or influential points.

Put the explanatory variable X on the horizontal axis and response Y on the vertical axis.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Covariance
Sample covariance measures joint movement:
s_{XY}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{n-1}.

Positive: variables tend to move in the same direction.
Negative: variables tend to move in opposite directions.
Magnitude depends on measurement units, limiting comparison.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Correlation
Correlation standardises covariance:
r=\frac{s_{XY}}{s_Xs_Y},\qquad -1\le r\le1.

Sign gives direction.
Magnitude gives strength of linear association.
Correlation is unit-free and symmetric in X and Y.

Excel: =CORREL(x_range,y_range).

Population model:
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_i+\varepsilon_i.

Least squares chooses the line that minimises:

Squaring prevents positive and negative residuals cancelling and penalises larger errors more strongly.
The fitted line describes the mean response predicted at each X.

R^2=\frac{\text{variation explained by the model}}{\text{total variation in }Y}.
Interpret R^2 as the percentage of sample variation in the response explained by its linear relationship with X.
It is not the percentage of observations predicted correctly.

text:
What hypothesis testing does
Hypothesis testing asks whether sample evidence is difficult to reconcile with a stated population benchmark.

Begin with a business claim.
Assume a null benchmark temporarily.
Measure how far the sample result is from that benchmark.
Quantify extremeness with a p-value.
Make a decision with a pre-selected significance level.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
The five-step workflow

State H_0 and H_1.
Calculate the test statistic.
Calculate the p-value in the correct tail or tails.
Compare the p-value with \alpha.
State a contextual conclusion about H_1.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Null and alternative hypotheses

H_0 contains equality and represents the benchmark.
H_1 expresses the claim being investigated.
Right-sided: H_1:\theta>\theta_0.
Left-sided: H_1:\theta<\theta_0.
Two-sided: H_1:\theta\ne\theta_0.

Choose direction from the question before seeing the result.

text:
Test statistic for a mean
When \sigma is unknown:
t=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt n},\qquad df=n-1.
The statistic is the observed difference measured in standard errors. Its sign indicates direction; its magnitude indicates distance from H_0.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
P-values and tails in Excel



Alternative
Excel p-value




H_1:\mu<\mu_0
T.DIST(t,df,TRUE)


H_1:\mu>\mu_0
1-T.DIST(t,df,TRUE)


H_1:\mu\ne\mu_0

The p-value is the probability—assuming H_0 is true—of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed, in the direction specified by H_1.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
section: Statistics vary from sample to sample
text:
Statistics vary from sample to sample
If we repeatedly take random samples of the same size, we get different values of \bar{x} and \hat p.
A sampling distribution describes those possible statistic values—not the distribution of individual observations.
This sampling variation is the uncertainty quantified by standard errors and confidence intervals.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Law of large numbers
As a random sample grows, the sample mean tends to settle closer to the population mean.

It does not say every larger sample is closer.
It does not repair biased sampling.
It describes long-run behaviour under repeated random sampling.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Central limit theorem
For sufficiently large random samples, the sampling distribution of the mean is approximately Normal:
\bar X\approx N\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\right).
The approximation concerns sample means, even when individual observations are not Normal.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Standard error of a mean
The standard deviation of the sampling distribution is the standard error:
SE(\bar X)=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\quad\text{or estimated by}\quad\frac{s}{\sqrt n}.
As n quadruples, the standard error halves. Precision improves with the square root of sample size.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:

For a sufficiently large random sample:
\hat p\approx N\left(\pi,\sqrt{\frac{\pi(1-\pi)}{n}}\right).

section: Point estimate plus margin of error
text:
Point estimate plus margin of error
Every confidence interval has the same architecture:
\text{estimate}\pm\text{critical value}\times\text{standard error}.

The point estimate identifies the centre.
The margin of error quantifies sampling uncertainty.
The confidence level controls the long-run coverage rate.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Known versus unknown \sigma
For a population mean:
\bar{x}\pm z^*\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\qquad(\sigma\text{ known}),
\bar{x}\pm t^*\frac{s}{\sqrt n}\qquad(\sigma\text{ unknown},\ df=n-1).
In business applications, \sigma is usually unknown, so the t interval is common.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics

z^*: =NORM.S.INV(1-alpha/2)
t^*: =T.INV(1-alpha/2,n-1)

For 95% confidence, z^*\approx1.96. A t^* value is larger for small samples and approaches 1.96 as n grows.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
section: From a business question to data
text:
From a business question to data
Consider: What influences the selling price of a house?

The business question determines what we need to observe.
Each row can represent one house.
Each column records a characteristic of those houses.
The appropriate statistical method depends on the kinds of variables involved.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Variables, observations, and data

A variable is a characteristic that can differ between items or individuals.
An observation is one item or individual on which variables are recorded.
Data are the observed values of those variables.

For a house:

variables might include suburb, number of bedrooms, and selling price;
one observation is one house; and
the recorded suburb, bedroom count, and price are its data values.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
The first classification decision
Variables are broadly classified as:

Categorical (qualitative): values indicate groups or labels.
Numerical (quantitative): values represent counts or measurements for which arithmetic is meaningful.

A number used as a label—such as a postcode—is still categorical.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Categorical variables
Nominal

Categories have no natural ordering.
Examples: payment method, suburb, product category.

Ordinal

Categories have a meaningful order.
Examples: poor/fair/good/excellent; low/medium/high risk.

The gaps between ordinal categories are not necessarily equal.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Numerical variables
Discrete

Produced by counting.
Often takes separate whole-number values.
Examples: number of purchases, complaints, or bedrooms.

Continuous

Produced by measuring.
Can potentially take any value within an interval.
Examples: waiting time, revenue, weight, or distance.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Cross-sectional and time-series data
Cross-sectional data

Observations on multiple entities at one time or during one period.
Example: sales across 50 stores in November.

Time-series data

Repeated observations of the same quantity through time.
Example: monthly sales for one store from January to December.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Descriptive and inferential statistics

Descriptive statistics organise, summarise, and present observed data.
Inferential statistics use sample evidence to learn about a wider population.

This week begins with description; later weeks develop inference.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Population, sample, parameter, statistic

Population: the complete group relevant to the question.
Sample: the subset actually observed.
Parameter: a numerical feature of the population.
Statistic: a numerical feature calculated from the sample.

A representative sample supports credible conclusions about the population.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
What is a “typical” value?
Measures of central tendency answer slightly different versions of this question:

Mean: the arithmetic balance point or average.
Median: the middle ordered value.
Mode: the most frequently occurring value or category.

The most appropriate measure depends on the variable and its distribution.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Mean
For observations x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n, the sample mean is

\bar{x}=\frac{x_1+x_2+\cdots+x_n}{n}.


Excel: =AVERAGE(range)
Uses every numerical observation.
Commonly used in later statistical analysis.
Sensitive to unusually large or small values.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Median
The median is the middle value after sorting observations from smallest to largest.

Excel: =MEDIAN(range)
Half the observations are at or below it and half are at or above it.
Resistant to extreme values.
Often informative for skewed variables such as income or house prices.

title: ETX1100/ETX5900 Business Statistics
text:
Mode
The mode is the value that occurs most frequently.

Excel for a single numerical mode: =MODE.SNGL(range)
Particularly meaningful for categorical or discrete data.
A dataset can have no mode or more than one mode.
For continuous data, the most populated interval may be more useful than one repeated value.

title: Assignment 1: The reception story
text:
The business case
You are a business analyst. Your company has launched the iPhone 4, and reports of reception signals dropping are attracting growing public criticism. The CEO will address the media in 48 hours. The Corporate Affairs team has commissioned you to analyse the available evidence and develop a persuasive, statistically defensible narrative. Your findings will inform the CEO’s public statemmeent. You must identify what the data demonstrate, what remains uncertain, and which claims the CEO can reasonably make.
The company wants to know whether the new model’s experience differs from that of the iPhone 3GS. A low rate of complaints or returns might reassure customers, while a higher rate of dropped calls or greater reception loss might require a more careful response. A persuasive data story must account for all of these measures, including those that complicate the message.
Use the simulated assignment workbook to prepare the briefing. Every customer record and measurement is simulated for teaching. The scenario is fictional; the workbook contains no actual company or historical customer data.

title: Assignment 1: The reception story
text:
Data and decision
The workbook has a Read me sheet with a data dictionary and two independent datasets:

Customer survey: a simple random sample of 2,000 purchasers of each model from the company’s fictional customer list, linked to support and returns records. Each row represents one purchaser. It records whether one observed call dropped, whether the purchaser reported a reception issue to customer support during the previous 30 days, and whether the phone was returned within 30 days for any reason. These are different events. Coverage and case use are also recorded.
Reception tests: a simple random sample of 100 distinct handsets of each model from fictional production batches, tested under the same simulated network conditions. Each handset has an ungripped and a gripped signal reading in dBm. Calculate reception loss = ungripped reading − gripped reading; a larger positive number means a greater loss. The two readings on a handset are paired, while the two model samples are independent.

The product team’s working rule is that a difference of 3 dB or more in average reception loss would be operationally important. This is a decision threshold for this fictional exercise, not a real engineering standard.
In the questions below, owner means an original purchaser, including someone who subsequently returned a phone. The survey deliberately samples the same number from each model. A probability calculated over all 4,000 records describes this balanced sample; it is not an estimate of the company’s overall purchaser mix without sales totals for both models.

title: Assignment 1: The reception story
text:
Your tasks

1. Describe the evidence (20 marks)

Identify the observational unit, population of interest, sample, and type of the main variables in each sheet. Explain why the survey and reception tests answer different questions.
Build a compact CEO evidence panel by model. Show the sample size; the rates of dropped calls, customer-support issue reports, and returns; and appropriate summaries of reception loss. Include two well-labelled charts: one comparing a customer outcome by model and one showing the distribution of reception loss by model. Use clear denominators and units so the panel could be understood in a media briefing.
Explain which headline figures would best answer the public concern and what a persuasive summary slide could conceal. In particular, distinguish a support-report rate from a call-drop rate and an all-cause return rate from a reception-related return rate. Identify one possible source of sampling or measurement bias.



2. Probability and reported issues (20 marks)
Using the Customer survey sheet, construct a contingency table for model and call_dropped. Show counts and relevant proportions. Calculate and interpret, as sample-based probability estimates:

P(\text{call dropped}\mid\text{iPhone 4});
P(\text{iPhone 4 and call dropped});
P(\text{reported issue}\mid\text{call dropped}); and
P(\text{call dropped or reported issue}).

State the denominator for each calculation. Compare the conditional call-drop probabilities for the two models and explain why this comparison alone does not establish that the handset model caused the difference. You may use a pivot table or Excel formulas; show enough working to make the calculations auditable.


3. Estimate uncertainty (20 marks)

Calculate a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of iPhone 4 owners in the fictional customer population who reported a reception issue in the previous 30 days. State the estimate, standard error, interval, assumptions, and interpretation. Compare the estimate descriptively with the iPhone 3GS sample proportion.
Calculate a 95% confidence interval for mean reception loss among iPhone 4 handsets in the fictional test population. State the estimate, standard error, interval, assumptions, and interpretation.
Explain one way sample size and one way sampling or test design affect how much confidence the team should place in these intervals.



4. Test the mean reception-loss claim (25 marks)
Use the Reception tests sheet to test, at the 5% significance level, whether the fictional iPhone 4 population has a greater mean reception loss than the fictional iPhone 3GS population.

State the parameter, null and alternative hypotheses, and why a one-sided, independent two-sample test is appropriate. Allow for unequal variances.
Show the sample means, standard deviations, sample sizes, estimated difference, test statistic or clear Excel test output, and p-value. If using Excel’s T.TEST, check that the observed difference is in the direction of the alternative before interpreting its one-tail p-value.
Give a decision and a plain-language conclusion. Distinguish statistical significance from the team’s 3 dB operational threshold. Explain a Type I error in this setting.



5. Advise Corporate Affairs and PR (15 marks)
Write a 150–250 word media-briefing recommendation for the Corporate Affairs and PR team. Propose a clear opening message for the CEO and two precise claims that the simulated evidence supports. Bring together the descriptive, probability, interval, and test results, including any result that complicates a reassuring message. Identify one claim the CEO should avoid, explain what remains uncertain, and recommend a next investigation or communication step. The team will use this advice to address public concerns, so write for a non-technical audience without overstating what the data prove.

title: Assignment 1: The reception story
text:
Submission
Submit one PDF brief (maximum 1,500 words, excluding tables, charts, and references) and one Excel workbook containing your calculations, pivot tables, and charts. The PDF should include the results needed to follow your argument; the Excel file is the audit trail. Label units, denominators, confidence levels, and hypotheses. Cite any external material you use.
